candidate.answerReason: Principal inverse ranges restrict solutions to [0, pi/2]. The equivalent equation sin(6x)=sin(x) has exactly the four listed solutions there.

methods.label: Use the principal ranges and equal-sine angles
methods.explanation:
First use the ranges of the inverse functions. Since \(x\in[0,\pi]\), we have \(\arccos(\cos x)=x\). Also, \(\arcsin\) returns values only in \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\), so any solution must satisfy \(0\le x\le\pi/2\).

On this smaller interval, \(\arcsin(\sin x)=x\). Consequently, the original equation is equivalent to
\[
\sin 6x=\sin x,
\qquad 0\le x\le\frac\pi2.
\]
The range restriction makes the converse valid: if the sines agree, their principal inverse sines agree as well.

On the unit circle, two angles have the same sine when their points have the same height. The angles are therefore either equal up to full turns or supplementary up to full turns. Thus, for an integer \(k\),
\[
6x=x+2k\pi
\quad\text{or}\quad
6x=\pi-x+2k\pi.
\]
The first family gives \(x=2k\pi/5\). Its interval restriction requires \(0\le k\le5/4\), so \(k=0,1\), giving \(0\) and \(2\pi/5\).

The second family gives \(x=(2k+1)\pi/7\). Here the restriction requires \(-1/2\le k\le5/4\), so again \(k=0,1\), giving \(\pi/7\) and \(3\pi/7\).

These four values are distinct, lie in \([0,\pi/2]\), and satisfy the sine equation, so each satisfies the original equation. The two angle families cover every possibility. There are \(\boxed{4}\) values, choice B.
methods.levelReason: Uses principal inverse ranges, unit-circle symmetry, periodicity, and elementary equations and bounds. No calculus is needed.

methods.label: Write the inverse-sine composition in pieces
methods.explanation:
For \(x\in[0,\pi]\), the principal inverse cosine gives \(\arccos(\cos x)=x\). Since the range of \(\arcsin\) is \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\), solutions can occur only for \(0\le x\le\pi/2\).

We can now describe \(\arcsin(\sin6x)\) explicitly. As \(6x\) runs from \(0\) to \(3\pi\), sine's symmetry and period give
\[
\arcsin(\sin6x)=
\begin{cases}
6x,&0\le x\le\pi/12,\\
\pi-6x,&\pi/12\le x\le\pi/4,\\
6x-2\pi,&\pi/4\le x\le5\pi/12,\\
3\pi-6x,&5\pi/12\le x\le\pi/2.
\end{cases}
\]
To justify these formulas, each expression on the right lies in the principal range on its stated interval and has sine equal to \(\sin6x\). It must therefore be the angle returned by \(\arcsin\).

Equating each piece to \(x\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
6x=x&\implies x=0,\\
\pi-6x=x&\implies x=\pi/7,\\
6x-2\pi=x&\implies x=2\pi/5,\\
3\pi-6x=x&\implies x=3\pi/7.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each candidate lies in its corresponding interval. Each linear piece contributes exactly one solution, and the four candidates are distinct. The pieces cover the entire possible interval, including its endpoints, so no other solutions remain. The answer is \(\boxed{4}\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Uses an explicit piecewise description derived from principal ranges and elementary sine identities, followed by four linear equations.
